11.0.0.en: 1 A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight. 2 When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom. 3 The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them. 4 Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death. 5 The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness. 6 The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness. 7 When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust men perisheth. 8 The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead. 9 An hypocrite with his mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered. 10 When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting. 11 By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked. 12 He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace. 13 A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. 14 Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety. 15 He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure.

11.0.1.en: Man practices righteousness in the field of work [1-4], so that the faithfulness of his heart and the sincerity of his intention are reflected in his work. He knows neither cheating nor deceit, whatever the material or moral temptation. He walks like his Creator and Savior, in a spirit of meekness and humility, without greed.

11.0.2.en: The effect of inner faithfulness extends to the field of personal problems [5-8]: how the righteous man comes out victorious in the midst of problems, troubles and afflictions.

11.0.3.en: It extends also to the field of government [9-15]: righteous citizens build a joyful society [10], an exalted one [11], pervaded by peace [12-13], and bearing the spirit of victory [14].

11.1.s.en: First: In the field of work

11.1.0.en: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" [1]

11.1.1.en: The literal translation of the Hebrew expression ba eben shelemak means "balances of stones," since stones were used in the scales.

11.1.2.en: Many make light of cheating in scales and measures, not knowing that it is an abomination in the eyes of the Lord, who cannot bear cheating and deceit.

11.1.3.en: * Every work that contains injustice is shameful, even in public affairs. False scales and unjust measures fall under the curse. If cheating in the market or in business brings a man under punishment, can it be overlooked when it is found in the midst of carrying out the duties of virtue?!

11.1.4.en: * Let each one weigh his words without cheating or deceit. "A false balance is abomination to the Lord." I do not mean that balance which weighs other things. Before the Lord this balance of words is hateful, which falsifies wise dignity while practicing deceit with cunning. God condemns the man who cheats his neighbor with treacherous injustice. He gains no profit from his skillful cleverness. For what does it profit a man if he gain the wealth of the whole world and deceive himself, so that he does not obtain eternal life?

11.1.5.en: St. Ambrose The disorder of man's scales, standards and concepts If sin has corrupted man's scales, standards and concepts, the incarnation of the wisdom of God has restored to man the truthfulness of his scales, measures and weights, so that man may give everything and every being its due, rendering unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's (Mt 22:21). Through the work of divine wisdom we have been given the possibility of restoring matters to their true scales, such as:

11.1.6.en: A. The balance between soul and body. God created for man true scales so that he might care for his whole being, working with his body with all its energies and abilities, and with his soul with all its possibilities. The soul takes the leadership of the body, so that man as a whole walks in the royal way. But sin made man lose his scales, and made the body a leader that rides the soul and directs it according to its evil lusts. The scales were upset, so that the rider became the ridden, and the ridden the rider. Therefore the wisdom of God came incarnate, and took our body, and He had a soul as a perfect man, so that in Him the body might be in harmony with the soul, and the two might walk the heavenly way.

11.1.7.en: By His incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension He opened the doors of heaven so that the Holy Spirit might dwell in man in his entirety, opening all his doors, to lead soul and body together in the heavenly pastures without conflict.

11.1.8.en: B. Sin upset man's scales in his view of earth and heaven, so he counted the earth his dwelling as one who will remain in it forever, and looked at heaven as an illusion or a fancy. He was no longer able to realize "Surely man walks about like a shadow" (Ps 39:6), for he counts the earth a reality worthy of all attention, while heaven and the eternal things are secondary matters. But the heavenly coming gave the believer's view a heavenly tinge, so that he sees the earth as if it had become heaven, and thanks God for his reality as a man living on earth, while his heart is in heaven.

11.1.9.en: C. Sin made man lose his true scales for weighing his spiritual, psychological, intellectual, scientific and social needs... so that he cannot realize the unity of life in order to balance all the aspects of his life, to be faithful in everything and sound in his personality. But when the Creator of soul and body, the unique Physician of man, became incarnate, He restored to life its unity, so that man might succeed in everything, by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, the Spirit of power and victory, not the spirit of failure.

11.1.10.en: D. The scales of man's thought were upset in his view of his own being, so he was no longer able to sit with himself and look into his inner depths, to discover the Kingdom of God within him, and to realize that God created him to make of him a dwelling for the Spirit of God. Man lost his awareness of his inner man, so that he saw in his life only the perishing of the outward man, without the growth and renewal of his inner man. But in Christ Jesus, who draws our gaze inward, saying to us, "The kingdom of God is within you," we have come to sing with the Apostle Paul: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16).

11.1.11.en: E. Our scales were upset even in our view of God, the world, the body and every heavenly and earthly creature, and our Christ, the incarnate Wisdom, came to offer us His Holy Spirit to grant us new scales through which we realize the following:

11.1.12.en: * God draws near to us in love; He is a Father even in His chastisements, opening His arms to us.

11.1.13.en: * The body is a holy talent, a divine gift, having its own sanctity, whether our own body or the bodies of others. So we do not look at it to satisfy fleshly lusts, but as a divine sanctuary in which the Lord delights.

11.1.14.en: * The world is a bridge by which we cross to the heavenly Jerusalem; we walk upon it as a divine gift. We accept sufferings as a school of philosophy and a way to enter into the fellowship of glory with our suffering Christ, as we also rejoice in every gift and blessing that stirs in us the spirit of thanksgiving and praise to God.

11.1.15.en: * The heavenly creation, for us, is the society of heaven in which we find friendships that last eternally.

11.1.16.en: * The earthly creation is talents with which we deal, so that we grow in the life of faithfulness, sharing with our Christ the quality of faithfulness.

11.1.17.en: F. Sin turned deceit and cunning into human wisdom, and faithfulness and truthfulness into narrowness of mind. Thus the scales were overturned, so that truth became falsehood in man's eyes, and falsehood truth! And the wisdom of God came to offer Himself, "the Truth," given in love through the Cross, which the Jews see as a stumblingblock and the Greeks as foolishness (1 Cor 1:23). In Christ Jesus we realize true wisdom.

11.1.18.en: G. Man's scales were upset by the spirit of selfishness, in which he sets up the ego as the center of the world, seeking what is his own. And "Love" Himself came to break the ego, in which there is a deadly selfishness, and to live in us Himself, so that our mind is opened and our heart widened, and we bear with our Christ, if possible, all people.

11.2.0.en: "When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" [2]

11.2.1.en: Creation was formed out of nothing, so in reality it has nothing to boast of before its Creator. Pride is a denial of the work of the Creator, who wishes to honor His rational creation and desires that it grow and be glorified continually. Humility, on the other hand, offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God the Creator, and acknowledges His kindness. Pride is a dangerous sign of folly and ruinous foolishness, while humility is a spiritual sign of steadfastness in the heavenly wisdom given to us as a free gift from the Creator.

11.2.2.en: When Nebuchadnezzar walked in the palace, and said in his arrogance: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?" (Dan 4:30), he was driven from men to live like the oxen. And when his reason returned to him and he blessed God and praised and honored Him, he says: "My reason returned unto me, and returned to the glory of my kingdom, my honour and brightness" (Dan 4:36).

11.2.3.en: The proud man shrivels up around himself, and thinks that he is the center of the world and of society, so he demands that all serve and respect him, supposing himself to be something. Then he finds others treating him otherwise than he expects, and he feels humiliation and shame, even in his own eyes. The humble man, however, does not wait for a word of praise, nor expect others to serve him, nor desire it, and behold, he is counted wise, receives honor and is the object of the love of many.

11.2.4.en: * It is pride that turns a man away from wisdom, and foolishness is the fruit of turning away from wisdom.

11.2.5.en: * "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." We read in the Holy Scripture of toil for temporal things: "All is vanity and vexation of spirit." The phrase "vexation of spirit," Presumption of spirit, means insolence, pride and arrogance, and it is also customary to say of the proud man that he has lofty spirits, and this is right, because the wind is called a spirit. And so it is written: "Fire and cold, snow and fog, the stormy wind" Spirit of tempest (Ps 148:8). Truly the proud man is called puffed up, as if he were exalted with the wind. And here the Apostle says: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1 Cor 8:1)...

11.2.6.en: Let us understand in truth that the poor in spirit are the humble and those who fear God, that is, those who have no spirit that swells.

11.2.7.en: In truth, the Beatitudes could not begin with anything other than this beginning, since they are set forth for the attainment of high wisdom: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (Ps 111:10), and on the other hand, "Pride is the first of sins" (Sir 10:15).

11.2.8.en: Therefore let the proud man seek earthly kingdoms and love them, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

11.2.9.en: St. Augustine * He who loves humility acquires many gifts through humility.

11.2.10.en: When you seek mercy, you find it among the humble, for humility is the dwelling place of righteousness.

11.2.11.en: Teaching is found with the humble, and knowledge is the springs of their lips.

11.2.12.en: Humility begets wisdom and understanding, and the humble acquire prudence...

11.2.13.en: Sweet is the word of the humble, and his face is radiant, and he laughs and rejoices.

11.2.14.en: Love is beautiful among the humble, and they know how to manage by it.

11.2.15.en: The humble fast from all evils, so their faces shine with the goodness of their hearts.

11.2.16.en: The humble man speaks and speech becomes him, and his lips laugh, yet the sound of his laughter is not heard...

11.2.17.en: The humble man humbles himself, but his heart is lifted to the heights above. Where his treasure is, there his thoughts are. The two eyes of his face look to the earth, and the two eyes of his mind to the heights above.

11.2.18.en: St. Aphrahat * Nothing is acceptable to God like a man's counting himself the last of all; this is the first principle of practical wisdom, for the humble man, wounded in his heart, does not love vainglory, nor is he angry, nor does he envy his neighbor, nor resort to any lust.

11.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of the treacherous is their shame" [3]

11.3.1.en: When a man seeks the truth with an upright conscience, the Holy Spirit of God works in him, leads him, guides him and accompanies him in the way of truth, as happened with Cornelius the pagan centurion. Since he was devout and feared the Lord, God sent him an angel to bid him seek Simon Peter, who would reveal to him the way of his salvation. And when Peter came, while he was speaking with him and with those present, "the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" (Acts 10:44).

11.3.2.en: The upright man is faithful to himself as to others, and so he finds his way clear and straight, while the treacherous or the cheat finds his way crooked, and loses the way, since he does not fulfill his mission.

11.3.3.en: David the prophet sings, saying: "My defence is of God, which saveth the upright in heart" (Ps 7:10). "The righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory" (Ps 64:10). It is also said: "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart" (Ps 97:11). "The upright shall dwell in thy presence" (Ps 140:13).

11.3.4.en: * God calls the sincere and truthful upright, those who hide nothing and do not conceal corruption beneath the surface.

11.3.5.en: Uprightness, as you see, is like this: God looks upon it above all things... Those who speak the truth need no effort, no struggle, no hypocrisy, no cunning, nor anything of the kind, because the truth shines through its own harmony.

11.3.6.en: In other words, just as deformed bodies need an outward artifice to cover their natural deformity, while natural beauty carries splendor in itself, so also falsehood can be distinguished from truth, and vice from virtue.

11.4.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death" [4]

11.4.1.en: The rich man often relies on his wealth, supposing that it achieves impossibilities for him.

11.4.2.en: But when the day of death comes, it is for the wicked a day of wrath and anger, and their wealth does not intercede for them, but is rather the cause of their condemnation, because they misused it. At that moment they cannot buy the forgiveness of sins, nor enjoy the divine mercies. The Book of Revelation describes the day of wrath thus: "And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and every mountain and island were moved out of their places. And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; and said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?" (Rev 6:14-17).

11.4.3.en: * I know why it is written: "Riches profit not in the day of wrath." This is said of the person who does not use his wealth for mercy. Is it not within the power of wealth to be used in time of need? In the hour when your spirit returns to the hands of God, you will understand that the benefit of all your wealth is to use it for mercy. For it was given to you by Jesus Christ, God and the Son of God.

11.4.4.en: St. Anba Shenouda * (Solomon) leads us toward understanding, especially when he says: "Riches profit not in the day of wrath." For he pours into your heart the knowledge that an abundance of money will not help you on that day, nor remove from you the eternal punishment. And when he says: [The righteous shall inherit the earth] (cf. Prov 2:21), he clearly means the earth which the meek also inherit. For the psalmist said first: "The meek shall inherit the earth" (Ps 37:11) LXX. And afterward the Lord said: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth" (Mt 5:4).

11.5.1.en: But the righteous man is saved from eternal death, for he enjoys the fellowship of eternal glory.

11.5.2.en: * "Many are the afflictions of the righteous (the just), but the LORD delivereth him out of them all" (Ps 34:19). Did He say: "Let Christians be righteous, and then those who hear my word will suffer no afflictions"? God did not promise this, but says: "Many are the afflictions of the just." Rather, when they are wicked their afflictions are fewer, and when they are righteous their afflictions are many. But after few afflictions, or with no afflictions, those (the wicked) go to eternal torment, from which they cannot escape. The righteous, however, after many afflictions come to eternal peace, where they no longer suffer any evil.

11.5.3.en: St. Augustine "The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness" [5]

11.5.4.en: The Book often confirms this truth, that righteousness is the believer's support, his deliverer, and his guide amid the afflictions of life, though it uses different words and expressions.

11.5.5.en: Palestine is known for its rocks and hills, so travelers find hardship in their journeys, but the guide is righteousness, for it leads the believer to eternal glory through the rocks of this life.

11.6.0.en: "The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in their own naughtiness" [6]

11.6.1.en: The corrupt man sets nets for himself in which he falls. But for the righteous, righteousness lifts up his feet, and the nets cannot catch him.

11.6.2.en: * An upright life and faith in God are a great weapon against the demons, who fear fasting, asceticism, night vigils and prayer, quietness and meekness, hatred of silver, boasting and humility, love of poverty and mercy, freedom from anger and the doing of righteousness in Christ, for the demons strive exceedingly not to be defeated. Let us remember in our hearts that the Lord is with us at all times, and the demons cannot do anything to us, and if they see that we are afraid and weak they make fear increase all the more in our hearts by their thoughts. But if they find us rejoicing in the Lord at all times, thinking in our hearts of the good things to come and speaking of the things of the Lord, and thinking: Everything is in the Lord's hand, then the demons can do nothing and have no authority in anything whatever. And if they find the soul fortified with such thoughts they are put to shame at once and turn back, for thus the enemy found Job fortified and steadfast and withdrew from him, when he could not turn his mind from God, and for this he was put to shame.

11.6.3.en: St. Anba Anthony * I marvel at the cunning of Satan, for though he is corruption and harm itself, he suggests thoughts that seem pure, but the result is a snare rather than a temptation.

11.6.4.en: St. Athanasius * If it happens that you are exposed to these evils, ask yourself: What are we doing in this world? Our time is short; your end is corruption and you are on the way to the grave. Then say to yourself: What are you doing there? Prostrate yourself before the Lord lest He condemn you to the eternal fire. Resist without truce the enemy who strikes you and destroys your understanding. Blessed are those who cross these dark and terrifying regions, this dreadful night, the desolate places, and this corrupt atmosphere of sin, and arrive at rest and gladness in the joy of the Holy Spirit.

11.7.0.en: St. Macarius the Great "When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust men perisheth" [7]

11.7.1.en: When a righteous man dies, his hope turns into a glorious reality, and no fear passes through him, nor does he fall into weakness; but the wicked man, who persists in impenitence in negligence, hoping for God's mercies, loses this vain hope by his death.

11.7.2.en: Hope is a great blessing for the striving spiritual man, who endures sufferings looking to the eternal glory prepared for him by God freely, but for the wicked, hope represents negligence and laxity. They walk in the way of destruction claiming that they will be saved and enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven, refusing to change their direction toward eternity; the hope of such people is nothing but a tomb.

11.7.3.en: * When a righteous man dies, hope does not perish. He hopes that his children will walk well, and hopes to receive great things. This statement also carries us over to thoughts concerning the resurrection, or to the generations that will come after us. Or it means that he who was righteous enjoys all these things already, and will enjoy their complete future fulfillment, and will finally enjoy the glory after death.

11.7.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * My son, before everything do not count yourself as anything, for this is the father of humility. And humility begets teaching, and teaching begets faith, and faith begets hope, and hope begets love, and love begets obedience, and obedience begets steadfastness without wavering.

11.7.5.en: * My son, hurry and take heed, lest you go astray and become lazy and negligent and be despised in the age to come. For it is written: Woe to the negligent, for their end has drawn near, and there is no helper for them, nor hope of salvation.

11.8.0.en: St. Anba Anthony "The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" [8]

11.8.1.en: Often the wicked man sets his snares for the righteous, and behold, he himself falls into them, and the righteous feels God's surpassing care for him.

11.8.2.en: When the wicked man rejects love and mercy, he throws himself into the hand of justice, and drinks of the cup he prepared for himself, supposing that he was offering it to his brother.

11.8.3.en: The cross which Haman prepared for Mordecai, Haman was hanged upon (Esth 7:9-10), and the lions' den which the accusers of Daniel planned in order to be rid of him, they and their families were cast into it and the hungry lions devoured them (Dan 6).

11.8.4.en: The Egyptians shed the blood of the children of the Israelites, and when the Egyptians were thirsty they found blood mingled with the water of the Nile. With the measure that a man measures to his brother it shall be measured to him.

11.9.1.en: "An hypocrite with his mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered" [9]

11.9.2.en: The hypocrite speaks other than what he hides within. So he destroys not himself alone, but draws his companion with him. It is as though wise Solomon were calling us to enjoy the spirit of discernment and to flee from the company of hypocrites, lest we perish with them.

11.9.3.en: * Do not bear ill will toward any man, lest your labors become vain.

11.9.4.en: * The worship of the man who has the malice of revenge in his heart is vain.

11.9.5.en: * This is our struggle: that we have no passion in the mouth, nor iniquity or malice in the heart.

11.9.6.en: Father Isaiah If hypocrites and deceivers perish by their words full of deceit, then the children of God can, by the spirit of discernment, escape the deceit of hypocrites as from the deceit of the enemy of good.

11.9.7.en: * The soul has a discernment from its rational sense by which it knows the difference between truth and falsehood, as the mouth distinguishes between wine and vinegar, though they are alike in color; so the soul by its rational sense knows the difference between spiritual gifts and satanic fantasies.

11.9.8.en: St. Macarius the Great * My son, do not speak in anger, but let your speech be with wisdom and knowledge, and your silence also, for our wise fathers' speech was full of wisdom and discernment, and so was their silence.

11.10.0.en: St. Anba Anthony "When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, there is shouting" [10]

11.10.1.en: If the hypocrite destroys his neighbor, the righteous man becomes a blessing to the whole city, not only by his guidance and counsels, but also by his prayers and supplications for others, and by the blessing of the Lord working in him. The Lord says: "Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know, and seek in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man, if there be any that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth; and I will pardon it?!" (Jer 5:1).

11.10.2.en: As for the wicked, when they die the righteous grieve over their destruction, but they shout for joy at the deliverance of the simple whom the wicked opposed in order to crush them.

11.11.0.en: "By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked" [11]

11.11.1.en: The righteous are a blessing not only to themselves and their families, but to the whole city.

11.11.2.en: St. Anthony the Great presents to us a wonderful picture of St. Pachomius, by whose blessing "the city is exalted," in his talk with the sons of St. Pachomius during their visit to him, when he said to them: [Let not your hearts be pained, my children, for the man of God, the righteous one adorned with every virtue, our father Pachomius, because he has fallen asleep, for you have become with him one body and partakers in the members (that is, the membership), and you have been filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit of God which used to shine within him. And truly I desired to see him in the flesh, and truly I was not worthy of him, especially since the souls which he gathered around him are holy to the Lord of Sabaoth, and these will show forth that they are higher than we, and walk in the way of the Apostles of Christ, which is the holy communion.]

11.11.3.en: * Pray, then, for the world, for "the eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry" (Ps 34:15). You know well that God hears the prayer of the righteous and that the supplication of a good man has great power, so remember us without ceasing.

11.11.4.en: St. Anba Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis Just as the city is blessed by the presence of the saints and their prayers, so it is also broken down by the mouth of the wicked, full of blasphemy and lying.

11.12.0.en: "He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace" [12]

11.12.1.en: Sometimes silence is the best thing we can do, especially if our words make us lose our peace, or wound our depths, or wrong others.

11.12.2.en: The foolish man lies in wait for the faults of others and concentrates on their weaknesses, so he despises them, but the wise man covers the weaknesses of his brothers and supports them in every positive aspect for their continual growth and edification.

11.12.3.en: * There is no work of love better than that a man should not despise his brother, as it is written: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him" (Lev 19:17). Accordingly, if you see your brother continuing in sin and you neglect to warn him so that he may then know his error, his blood will be required of you. But if he repeats the sin and continues in it, he dies in his sin, and it is good for you to heal him with love without wounding him and without scorning him as an enemy.

11.12.4.en: Abba John the Short * If you pray and no evil thing comes into your mind, you have become free. He who blames his brother, or despises him, or speaks against him before others, or shows anger toward him, is far from mercy. And if a man says that he wants to repent of his sins and he does any of these things, he is a liar.

11.13.0.en: St. Anba Isaiah "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" [13]

11.13.1.en: The faithful man does not disclose the secrets entrusted to him, unless in doing so there is edification for their souls and within the proper limits for the salvation of others, not to expose them.

11.13.2.en: * Frown at the one who begins to speak against his brother before you, for if you do so you will be guarded before God and before him.

11.14.0.en: St. Isaac the Syrian "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety" [14]

11.14.1.en: Total reliance on one's own judgment is the height of folly, for even the wisest and most devout of men have their grave errors, and sometimes an inability to discern. No man is immune from error. Man needs to seek God's counsel and to resort to a spiritual father or spiritual guide. Rehoboam lost most of the kingdom because he ignored this important truth, and many have suffered grave harm for the same reason.

11.14.2.en: It is fitting for the believer not to rely on his own idea and feelings, but to consult and discuss in a spirit of humility and a sincere desire to benefit from the abilities and experiences of others.

11.14.3.en: The Book of Daniel tells us of Nebuchadnezzar's need for a wise counselor from God, and when the secret was revealed to him the king glorified the God of Daniel (Dan 2:46). King Belshazzar also needed a counselor (Dan 5:13).

11.14.4.en: * Since we all wish to come out of Egypt and flee from Pharaoh, we certainly need another Moses, a mediator from God and before God, who by standing for us between action and knowledge (contemplation) stretches out the arms of prayer to God, until those whom he leads cross the sea of their sins, and overcome Amalek (Ex 17), and raise the banner of victory. For he is deceived who surrenders himself to this way (the monastic way) and imagines that he needs no one to lead and guide him.

11.14.5.en: St. John Climacus * An elder said: [A rich man distributed all his possessions, freed his slaves and renounced the world, then came to rely on himself, being his own guide, and decided not to be a follower of another nor to learn from one who was older than he, and he fell into hideous impurities and nearly perished had not God by His grace rescued him through repentance, so that he learned by experience that humility is greater than works.]

11.14.6.en: The Garden of the Monks * If (the believer) does not walk with his guide from the beginning to the end, he will never reach the city. So cast your will behind you and be humble, and you will be saved.

11.15.0.en: St. Barsanuphius "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure" [15]

11.15.1.en: He has already spoken of not being hasty in standing surety for a stranger, without examination and good management, whether as to the truth of his need, the study of his use of the loan, and the ability of the borrower and the surety to repay (cf. Prov 6:1-5).

11.15.2.en: The wise man is afraid of rashness in standing surety for a stranger who has come to spend a night or a day in order to borrow, with no guarantees of repayment, or no seriousness about repaying.

11.15.3.en: But our Christ signed with His blood on the wood of the Cross, standing surety for us. He paid the price of our sins, death, and He is able to repay. The Apostle Paul says: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sakes he became poor, though he was rich, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor 8:9). He became surety for us strangers, to remove our estrangement. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19). In His surpassing love He says: "Then I restored that which I took not away" (Ps 69:4), for He paid our debts which He had not borrowed, and so through Him we have become free.

11.16.0.en: 16 A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches. 17 The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh. 18 The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward. 19 As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death. 20 They that are of a froward heart are abomination to the LORD: but such as are upright in their way are his delight. 21 Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered. 22 As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion. 23 The desire of the righteous is only good: but the expectation of the wicked is wrath. 24 There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. 25 The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. 26 He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it. 27 He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him. 28 He that trusteth in his riches shall fall; but the righteous shall flourish as a branch. 29 He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: and the fool shall be servant to the wise of heart. 30 The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise. 31 Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner.

11.17.s.en: A. A woman's grace brings honor

11.17.0.en: "A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong men retain riches" [16]

11.17.1.en: In the Septuagint: "A gracious woman raises honor for her husband, but she who hates righteous things is a throne of dishonor." The meaning is that because of a devout and wise wife her husband is honored, but she who does not care for her eternity and salvation becomes a seat of shame, and everyone who clings to her loses his honor. It is as though the wise man here urges a man to choose a life partner who is gracious and devout.

11.17.2.en: The strong, or the physically powerful, are often able to work in order to enjoy wealth, as well as to protect it from those who try to rob or seize it. So by grace and meekness a woman can gain honor and esteem in the eyes of many. There is nothing more beautiful in a woman than the touch of grace and the anointing of humility, meekness and gentleness together with wisdom. This is what David the prophet perceived in the person of Abigail, when he said to her: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: and blessed art thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand" (1 Sam 25:32-34).

11.17.3.en: So Ruth the Gentile was able to find grace in the eyes of God, who chose that the Word of God should come incarnate from her seed, and in the eyes of the people. And as Boaz said to her: "For all the gates of my people do know that thou art a virtuous woman" (Ruth 3:11).

11.17.4.en: * In speaking of the glory of the man, Paul now sets up a balance, so that the man may not boast beyond what is fitting, nor oppress the woman. For in the Lord the woman is not independent of the man, neither is the man independent of the woman. If you ask who came after the other, each is the cause of the other, or rather, not each is from the other, but God is the cause of all.

11.17.5.en: * The women stood at the Cross, the weaker sex, which appeared stronger, and so all things were completely changed.

11.18.s.en: B. A man's mercy benefits himself

11.18.0.en: "The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel breaketh his flesh" [17]

11.18.1.en: What a man does to others he offers to himself; the mercy he practices toward others leads him to enjoy the divine mercies, and gains him inner peace. And he who thinks he is crushing others by his violence is crushing himself without knowing it. The cup we fill for others we are bound to drink ourselves.

11.18.2.en: * What is purity? It is a heart full of mercy toward all the natures of creation.

11.18.3.en: * The prayer of the hateful is like seed sown upon a rock. A merciless ascetic is like a tree without fruit.

11.18.4.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Be desirous of good things and keep them, a servant pleasing to your Master, a humble disciple of Him who for your sake humbled Himself, an obedient disciple of the Obedient, enduring with the Enduring, longsuffering with the Longsuffering, merciful for the sake of the Merciful, bearing the burdens of your neighbor as He Himself bore your burdens, loving all sincerely as He Himself loved us, following Him in all things until He receives you into His great rest, where "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1 Cor 2:9).

11.19.s.en: C. Sowing righteousness gives a true reward

11.19.0.en: "The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward" [18]

11.19.1.en: The wise man links evil with deceit, and righteousness with faithfulness. For evil carries within it a deception of the soul and of the inner sight, so that the wicked man imagines in sin a joyful life, happiness, wealth or honor. And the righteous man, or the just, sees in faithfulness to God and to himself as to men the secret of his inner happiness. Evil carries within it its corrupt fruit, and righteousness carries within it its reward.

11.19.2.en: The clear example of this serious contrast is Sennacherib king of Assyria and Hezekiah. The first, in his wickedness, used to reproach God and speak against Him with insolence and arrogance. He says: "As the gods of the nations of other lands have not delivered their people out of mine hand, so shall not the God of Hezekiah deliver his people out of mine hand" (2 Chr 32:17). But devout Hezekiah, the man of prayer, enjoyed deliverance from the hand of Assyria from heaven itself.

11.19.3.en: The wicked man reaps the deceit with which he thought he was deceiving others, and finds that he is cheating himself. But he who is diligent in sowing the seeds of righteousness finds a sure reward.

11.20.0.en: "As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death" [19]

11.20.1.en: True holiness is real life and happiness, but he who runs after evil is only running to end his life.

11.21.s.en: E. Walking without crookedness gives us joy in the Lord

11.21.0.en: "They that are of a froward heart are abomination to the LORD: but such as are upright in their way are his delight" [20]

11.21.1.en: There is nothing the Lord cannot bear like hypocrisy and crookedness, and nothing the Lord loves like uprightness and holiness.

11.22.s.en: F. Collective action does not justify evil

11.22.0.en: "Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered" [21]

11.22.1.en: The wicked joining together does not protect them from the fruit of their evil, but the righteous, they and their seed who walk in their likeness, enjoy divine protection.

11.23.s.en: G. A woman's beauty is in her mind

11.23.0.en: "As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion" [22]

11.23.1.en: A woman often destroys her beauty by her lack of wisdom, so that she is like one who takes a gold ring and puts it in the nose of a sow.

11.23.2.en: J. Vernon McGee says: [Have you seen a sow walking around with a gold ring in her snout? Well, there are many of them here in... They are beautiful women without discretion.]

11.23.3.en: If God has given many women bodily beauty, what gives this beauty its dignity and worth is discretion, wisdom and discernment.

11.23.4.en: Gold signifies the heavenly life that will not corrupt. The true believer is bound to walk with a practical heavenly mind, and if he deviates he is like the sow that wallows in the mire, and so defiles the gold ring in her snout (her nose).

11.23.5.en: * Although it is believed that virginity is something exceedingly precious and has a divine appearance, yet if the life as a whole is not in harmony with the soul, virginity becomes "a jewel of gold in a swine's snout," or "a pearl trodden under the feet of swine."

11.23.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Those whom you indicate do not possess the knowledge which none but the pure possess, but acquire a vain knowledge of which the Apostle speaks, saying: "Avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Tim 20:6). Those who appear to receive some kind of knowledge, or those who devote their souls to reading the sacred volumes and memorizing the Holy Scriptures without abandoning fleshly sins, of these it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion" (Prov 11:22). For what does it profit a man if he acquires the heavenly adornment of eloquence, and the costly beauty of the Holy Scripture, if he corrupts it by clinging to filthy deeds and evil thoughts, pushing them into unclean ground, or defiling them by wallowing in the filth of his lusts?! The result is that what is an ornament for those who use it well becomes for them not only unable to adorn them but filth and increasing mire, for "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner" (Sir 15:9). For it is said to him by the prophet: "What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?!" (Ps 50:16). Such souls have not the fear of the Lord in any way, for it is said: "The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom" (Prov 15:33). And yet they try to draw out the meanings of the Holy Scripture by continual meditation on it, and fittingly they are asked in the Book of Proverbs: "Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding?" (Prov 17:16).

11.23.7.en: Father Nestor * In brief, if anyone thinks he becomes beautiful by gold, he is less than the gold, and he who is less than gold is not lord over it. But for a person to confess that he is less beautiful than the mine in (the region of) Lydia, how ugly! If gold is spoiled by the filth of a sow stirring up the mire with her snout (her nose), so also these women who luxuriate excessively in their pleasure, exulting in wealth, spoil what is truly beautiful, through the defilement of servility to fleshly lusts.

11.24.s.en: H. The goal of the righteous is good for all

11.24.0.en: "The desire of the righteous is only good.

11.24.1.en: The expectation of the wicked is wrath" [23]

11.24.2.en: What the wicked hope for is the harming of others, while the righteous desire good for all; every man receives in himself what he desires for others, and what he seeks for his brother returns to him.

11.24.3.en: When man's heart is planted in the Lord who is all good, the heart overflows with longing to do good to every man as far as he can. Therefore the psalmist commands us: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Ps 37:4).

11.25.0.en: Giving in truth is receiving, and generosity in giving is wealth and prosperity, and giving rest to others brings rest to us. The Lord Christ says: "Give, and it shall be given unto you..." (Lk 6:38).

11.25.1.en: And the Apostle says: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth with blessings shall reap also with blessings. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:6-7).

11.25.2.en: "There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty" [24]

11.25.3.en: He who cares to give to the poor, God blesses everything to which his hands are stretched, so that he increases in wealth and blessing, but he who refrains from giving because of his stinginess and miserliness loses the Lord's blessing and is counted poor.

11.25.4.en: * The demons gather secretly against you like the Egyptians, and the devil their chief like Pharaoh, and they besiege you with worries and thoughts that darken your soul and deprive you of seeing the light of the knowledge of Christ.

11.25.5.en: And these are the thoughts which they begin to stir up in your mind:

11.25.6.en: Why did you leave the world, where you could easily have become righteous?

11.25.7.en: Why did you squander your wealth, from which you used to give alms when it was at your side?

11.25.8.en: Now that you have distributed it hastily and prematurely, perhaps it was given to those who do not deserve it. If you had kept it and invested it wisely, you could now entertain strangers, ease the pains of the weary, clothe the naked, help the monks and solitaries with your gifts, and stand by the widows and orphans; your house would have become a place for all good works; for as long as your money was at your side it helped you to rest and to relieve the pains of others.
